rss.summary: My obituary for programming Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code: Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible. If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving. rss.title: Advancing coding in low‑resource programming languages
rss.summary: Learn how OpenAI is improving ChatGPT across low-resource programming languages, with new evaluations for software engineering, SQLite, and COBOL migration.
rss.text_excerpt:
Our latest model advances bring stronger capabilities for building and migrating software in low-resource programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic. These languages have less code and documentation available for models to learn from than languages like Python and JavaScript, yet support critical infrastructure and essential services around the world. COBOL supports ⁠ (opens in a new window) more than 40% of online banking systems, 80% of in-person credit card transactions and 95% of ATM transactions, while Fortran is used in weather forecasting ⁠ (opens in a new window) and nuclear reactor safety analysis ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Improving AI’s ability to work in these languages could help teams maintain and modernize the software that essential services depend on. This work is guided by feedback from developers and enterprise customers who have told us that coding models often struggle with these languages. Maintaining and modernizing this software can be difficult: documentation may be incomplete, original developers may have left the company, and important business rules may only exist in code. Whether teams are fixing bugs or migrating to another language, they need to preserve the behavior their systems depend on. To measure progress, we developed two evaluations. MultiLangBench tests whether a model can build a SQLite-compatible database engine from scratch across 20 different programming languages. Our COBOL migration evaluation tests whether a model can migrate existing programs to another language while preserving their behavior. Together, they test two complementary skills: building new software and preserving what existing software does. Our latest models show substantial improvements across both evaluations, delivering much higher accuracy at lower cost. On MultiLangBench, GPT‑6 Astra achieves an average test pass rate of 87.4% across 20 programming languages, up from 26.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, with improvements in every language tested. GPT‑6 Luna also outperforms GPT‑5.6 Sol, reaching 40.3% at approximately 78% lower estimated API cost. On our COBOL migration evaluation, GPT‑6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with just 5.4% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, while costing 39% less. rss.title: Meta shakes up the frontiers, open and closed
rss.text_excerpt:
This has been a week where the balance of American open-weight models took a step change back toward the frontier. Meta took the lead of this charge with Muse Spark Open , which is now the strongest American-made open model by quite some margin, but the addition of Reflection’s first model Beam is also relevant. Without these two models, there would be 20+ open-weight models built and released by Chinese companies better than the best Western models. At the time of writing this, Mistral has also announced a strong model, Mistral Large 4 , with an index score of 38 (see below), but its weights are not yet released. There are rumors of a few more strong American open-weight models coming from other organizations too! In many ways, the gap between the best American and Chinese models has been reduced roughly by half. We’ve gone from the best American open models being largely irrelevant to consumers who require the cutting edge of performance, to them being behind but relevant. This paints the picture of the cut-throat, competitive nature of the frontier model business. Reflection and Mistral announced their model scores and Meta dropped the weights of a smarter model before these other two labs could get their own weights out. All of these models are competing with Chinese models released months ago, where the industry is collectively asking — where have Kimi and Zhipu AI been since the releases of GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 on Aug. 18th and Jul. 16th, respectively? That is a very nuanced question, which I’ll dig into another time. Today’s piece is focused on Meta’s turnaround, what Muse Spark Open means for the ecosystem, and the balance of power across Western frontier labs. We are piloting a new show on Latent Space: High Taste Testers, a variant of our food show where we pull you in to a typical lunch conversation in San Francisco. All your favorite talking points, starting with Dev Day and going into the latest models and assistants, are here: Let us know your feedback! AI News for 10/15/2026-10/16/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! US Open-Weights Push: Muse Spark Open and Reflection Beam Muse Spark Open (Meta) : An 816B-total, 42B-active MoE with open weights. Artificial Analysis scores it 39 on its Intelligence Index, the highest for a US open-weights model and 13 points above NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL at 26 ( AA ). Architecture and footprint : 62 layers, GQA with 16 KV heads, 8 of 256 experts active per token, a 1.8B Perception Encoder and 1M context. Inputs are text, image, video and audio; output is text. BF16 weights are about 1.6TB. Meta’s NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes only the experts, cutting weights to about 530GB. Meta says that fits on 4 Blackwell Ultra GPUs, 8 H200s or two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios. Pricing and efficiency : Together, Fireworks and Baseten charge $1.25/$4.25 per M input/output tokens, with $0.15 cached input. AA puts the cost at $0.84 per index task, versus $2.01 for GLM-5.3 and $0.27 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. It uses 40k output tokens per task, the fewest among the top nine open models ( cost ). Vals counts 55.5M output tokens across its index, the fewest of any open model, but says input tokens drive most of its cost ( Vals ). Weak spot : It ranks last among the top nine open models on AA’s four agentic evals while leading open models on AA-Omniscience. Vals places it #12 among open-weight models and #38 overall ( Vals ). Arena ranks it the top US open model on Code Arena WebDev with 1511 points, #13 among open models ( Arena ). License : The custom Muse Model License requires “Built with Muse Spark Open” attribution. Model-as-a-Service businesses with more than $20M in annual revenue need a separate agreement with Meta. Sign up · Docs · Book demo · Website · Feature requests · Contribute · Hiring


Macro is the all-in-one workspace for you and your team. It unifies email + messages + docs + tasks + agents + CRM into a single fast interface with shared team-level memory. Everything in your workspace is @linked and searchable so your team (and your agents) never have to switch tools.
# Why Macro We built Macro because we wanted a single operating system for our startup. There are many good software products, and we used them all — Slack, Linear, Notion, HubSpot, and Superhuman — but they don't work together as one system. As we scaled our last venture to ~20 people things started to break: every team got their own tools and the company was held together by MCP and Zapier. The company was not computable. It was chaotic. Macro is a complete redesign of work software from the ground up as a single system. Designed by us in NYC and Toronto, dogfooded by our team of ~15 for two years. Built in SolidJS and Rust for speed and reliability. We're focused on building something that any small company or team at a larger company can use as their "operating system".
# Features Macro is composed of 'blocks' designed to be modular, extensible, and work together like Lego. For each block, we studied the best prior art and tried to make it even better. github.text_excerpt: # RockBot An event-driven autonomous agent framework. --- ## What is RockBot? RockBot is a framework for building **multi-agent AI systems** where agents communicate exclusively through a message bus. There is no shared memory, no direct method calls between agents, and no LLM-generated code running in-process with the host. Agents built using the RockBot framework SDK are designed with the principle of least priviledge: an agent should not have access to any secrets other than LLM keys. All other secrets should be in MCP servers or other isolated services. Each agent is an isolated process that reacts to messages, invokes tools, calls LLMs, delegates work to other agents, and emits responses — all via a topic-based pub/sub message bus backed by RabbitMQ (or an in-process bus for local development).
